utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. And to you Madam Registrar, if you would call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, all the accused are here. Amongst the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and is Mr. Sarapa here or not? No. He is absent too. Mr. Petrusic is here. For the Prosecution it's Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Vanderpuye. So, welcome back. We do have a lot of issues that we could raise but we have every intention to proceed with as much celerity as possible and necessary break these down into parts. Today we'll deal with those which are more urgent and more relevant to this and the next couple of sittings. May we remind you, with some emphasis, to your obligations pursuant to our order concerning the presentation of evidence and the conduct of parties during the Defence cases which we issued on the 26th of May? Pursuant to paragraph 3(A) of that order, within seven days of the provision of the list of witnesses for June by the Popovic team, the Prosecution and the remaining Defence teams were obliged to provide an estimate of the total time expected to be taken cross-examining each witness. Now, it seems that not everyone has grasped the idea and also the procedure that needs to be followed. Some of you have sent an e-mail to the Senior Legal Officer, Prosecution provided provisional time estimate for cross-examination. Other have just informed the Senior Legal Officer without an indication of even whether the Prosecution was being informed and Mr. Zivanovic was being informed, so we would like you, please, to follow the following procedure. Your position needs to be communicated formally by means of a filing. That's how we would like you to do it. At the end of the day between sending an e-mail to the Senior Legal Officer and making a proper filing, there isn't much difference. But it would enable us to make sure that everyone is properly informed. Again, paragraph 3(B) of the order states that by 5 p.m. on Friday of each week during the Defence case, the Prosecution and the remaining Defence teams shall provide the Trial Chamber and other parties with an estimate of total time to be expected to be taken cross-examining each witness. Now, the Prosecution filed a notice in time giving its estimate and the Nikolic and Miletic teams sent e-mails. Borovcanin and Gvero filed theirs on Sunday, which was beyond the time limit. Please, again, we are not -- we don't intend to make a mountain out of this mole hill but please stick to the timeframes that we have indicated and if possible use the form of filing. There is -- I move on to a motion from Mr. Zivanovic, which I will refer to as the Popovic Defence team Rule 92 bis motion. We are going to rule on this orally now. On the 19th of May 2008, the Popovic Defence team filed a confidential motion for admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis in which he proposed to admit the statements of six witnesses without cross-examination. That motion appears to have been modified according to the Trial Chamber by Mr. Zivanovic's subsequent filing of a notice concerning the witnesses schedule and the estimated time for their examination on the 23rd of May 2008. In the notice, the Popovic Defence team notes that one of the six witnesses, Danilvic -- Danojlovic will testify as a viva voce witness for Pandurevic. Popovic also states that he will move to convert another of the witnesses, that is Vukicevic to viva voce status based upon the Prosecution's initial opposition. The Popovic Defence team also appears to indicate that he will call another of these witnesses, that is Witness Ilic, for viva voce testimony. In its response, which was filed on the 28th of May 2008, the Prosecution did not oppose the admission of any of the six statements. It does, however, note that it wishes to cross-examine both Ilic and Danojlovic and that it does not wish to cross-examine witness Vukicevic. The Trial Chamber construes the Popovic Defence team motion and his subsequent notice as withdrawing his Rule 92 bis requests to admit the statements of witnesses Danojlovic and Ilic. As to the remaining four witnesses, at issue in the motion, the Prosecution does not oppose the admission of their statements and does not seek to cross-examine any of them. The Trial Chamber has reviewed the statements and has determined that each is appropriate for admission without cross-examination pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Accordingly, the statements of witnesses Vukicevic, Jusufovic, Mazibrada, and Vlaisavljevic are provisionally admitted without cross-examination pending their receipt in a form that fully complies with the requirement of Rule 92 bis(B). Is that clear to you, Mr. Zivanovic? You need to follow this formality before they can actually be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, we have cleared that as well. Now, there was -- Mr. Haynes and Mr. McCloskey, accused Pandurevic filed a motion on the 26th of May 2008, to amend his 65 ter list by adding one document. Then subsequently three days later, on the 29th of May, Popovic's Defence team filed a similar motion, namely to amend his Rule 65 ter exhibit list with five exhibits pertaining to Witness that I'm not going to mention here. My understanding and the information that the Trial Chamber has received based on the information that the Trial Chamber has received, is that the opposition does not oppose these two motions. I just want a confirmation of that following which we'll proceed with granting the two motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and I ask you for the record, not because I wanted to verify. Having heard you, Mr. McCloskey, we grant both motions considering that there are justified and no opposition is forthcoming from the Prosecution. Now, when we had the Pre-Defence Conference, you will recall that we had discussed at some length a problem, an issue, pending between the Prosecution and the Popovic Defence team about whether the Popovic Defence team had provided the Prosecution with proper adequate 65 ter witness summaries. I am informed, and again you will need to confirm this to me, that an agreement has been reached and that the Prosecution has no further reason to uphold or continue with their objection or with their presentation to the Trial Chamber. Is that correct, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have no further objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm assuming then that you are going to formally withdraw this motion. You can withdraw it orally here if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'll -- I withdraw that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think we have covered what is -- what was more urgent for the purpose of this sitting. I will soon be proceeding with the admission of the first witness, but I take it, Mr. Zivanovic, that you want to address the Chamber before that and I also see -- one moment, because Ms. Fauveau is quicker than both of us. Yes. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would just like to tell you that I informed my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic, that I had a very brief intervention before he starts. I would like to talk about the order regarding the order of the cross-examinations so I would like to ask you before the first witness begins to testify, I would like you to clarify a point in this order. According to the order, the parties who have already cross-examined a witness may have a redirect when a new topic is raised during the examination-in-chief led by the Prosecutor. The clarification that I would like to ask you to make is the following: The Defence, after the examination-in-chief of the Defence, says that they have no questions and if during the cross-examination of the Prosecutor a particular issue is -- arises, would the Defence have the right to put additional questions after the cross-examination of the Prosecutor even if they had not cross-examined previously the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are not going to provide you with a general rule applicable throughout the entire trial. We'll entertain such requests if and when they arise, and they will be decided on whether it's in the interest of justice to grant or not to grant. That's the position. So Mr. Zivanovic, you asked some weeks ago to -- for an opportunity to make an opening statement, which you have now. Please go ahead. After that, we'll bring your first witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence team of Vujadin Popovic is in the unique position to begin presentation of its case, uncertain that the Prosecution has ended the presentation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please read slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Such position requires corresponding opening statement. In the first place, although we have got the green light to appeal the decision to reopen the Prosecution case, I'm going to state in the open court how it badly affected the Defence of my client. By doing so, I do not intend to elaborate the factual and the legal arguments, since it will be done in our appeal. But the interest of justice and the right of my client for a fair trial compels me to summarise very briefly serious impact on the right of my client to have a fair trial. Five weeks after conclusion of its case, the Prosecution asked to reopen it on the ground of new evidence on the events unrelated for the acts from the indictment. It was done while the Defence was fully engaged in preparation of its case and despite a relevance of such evidence for preparation of our Defence, the Prosecution decided not to disclose it for whole four weeks. It seriously affected the right of my client to a fair trial in two ways. First of all, our unawareness misled us not to direct our attention toward new evidence, to rearrange our Defence strategy and find corresponding evidence. Moreover, the Prosecution decided to disclose this evidence not before our Defence submitted military expert report. In the second place, unlike the other Defence teams, we had to divide our attention in next three weeks between the preparation of our Defence and challenging the motion to reopen the Prosecution case. But despite of all mentioned disadvantages, we shall begin this morning the presentation of our evidence. Due to uncertainty as to reopening of the Prosecution case, I shall not address in this opening statement acts and conduct of the accused, but only the crime base to the extent that we dispute. But before the listing these issues, I want to state clearly that our defence does not deny the large but still unknown number of Muslim men was executed after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995. It was apparently a serious crime punishable under both national and international law. However, we strongly deny that such crime amounts to genocide. Similarly, we dispute the charge from paragraph 25 of the indictment, that VRS and MUP forces murdered over 7.000 Muslim men and boys. Our submission is that such allegations have been widely and unnecessarily exaggerated to meet one of the requirements for genocide charge. Therefore, in the course of our case, we shall bring several experts who will challenge the findings of the Prosecution demography, DNA and forensic expert witnesses. Our Defence also denies that Srebrenica ever became a safe area in the true sense of the term. We shall demonstrate that the decent intent of United Nations Security Council to protect civilian population from the war sufferings was perverted by decision of B and H authorities to keep their its 6.000 people strong units. We shall prove that from the onset of the Bosnian war until the very end of the enclave, Srebrenica was the focal point of organised subversive activities against both civilian and military targets on the territory of Republika Srpska. We shall document that B and H authorities forbade Muslim civilians to leave the enclave preventing and punishing all those who attempted to do that. We shall prove that it was done both in order to provide cover from potential retribution anticipated after attacks on surrounding Serbian villages and to provide logistic by misappropriation of humanitarian aid designated for the civilian population. It is our submission that VRS had a full right to neutralise such constant, two years long threat. Consequently, we submit that operation Krivaja 95 was a legitimate military operation against enemy forces undertaken just after all other means for disarming 28th Division were ineffective. We further submit that the movement of Muslim civilians displaced in Potocari and disported to the B and H territory was a result of explicit request made by civilians and conveyed to General Mladic by DutchBat commander. Refusal of such request meant the prohibition to civilians to leave the enclave and would be a serious crime against their freedom of movement. Accordingly, I strongly oppose to the language of the indictment describing the acts in Potocari as separation of the Muslim men and boys from their families. We have demonstrated that the ABiH soldiers, disguised in civilian cloth, were mingled among the refugees in Potocari. We shall document that the VRS had legitimate right to isolate and arrest all suspected enemy soldiers, and they did it. There is no arrest without separation of detained individuals from those who remain free, including their families. The language of the Prosecution avoids saying clearly that VRS arrested the Muslim men in Potocari as suspected enemy soldiers, being aware of legitimacy of such act. It, however, charges the accused with legitimate and unavoidable consequence of such act, the separation of arrested people from those who remained free. By stating this, I would like to emphasise that subsequent maltreatments, abuses and executions of detainees were completely illegal acts, punishable both under national and international law. But their detention was legal. Our Defence will also prove that all Muslim men in Srebrenica, from 16 to 65 years of age, were eligible and mobilised into armed forces according to the B and H laws. We shall argue that they left Srebrenica on 11 July 1995 to Jaglici and Susnjari complying with the orders of competent Srebrenica. In support of this submission I show the inspection of the brigade from the 8th Operative Group carried out on the second anniversary of the ABiH in May 1994. This video depicts the unarmed Muslim men, all in civilian clothes, arrayed in the various brigades of the 8th operation group of ABiH. The video was obtained in the course of our investigation from the association of the former camp inmates of Republika Srpska. It has not been translated yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anything wrong? I see. Okay. Do you want to proceed with this? Because I think it makes very little sense going through it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have a problem with sound, but the video depicts those brigades consisting just of men in civilian clothes arrayed and presented as a various brigade members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You will be producing this in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, despite of military character of the column breaking through the territory held by VRS, it was not attacked while past the first line of Srebrenica encirclement. At the time, it clearly demonstrated the absence of an intent on the part of VRS to kill all the Muslim men from the column and specific intent to commit genocide in corroboration of this submission you will see the statement of B and H Prime Minister, Hasan Muratovic in his speech on the session of the B and H parliament held in August 1995, discussing the causes of the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa. The whole session was recorded on two CDs, and I will ask to play it from --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid we have again the problem with sound. Excuse me, may we have a very short break for two or three minutes to resolve this sound problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ready to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we are. We will go back to the inspection of the 28th Division units.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Since the audio is too poor to interpret from, we are merely reading out the B/C/S transcript provided by the Defence. "The material strengthening of the military forces successful fulfilment of tasks and functional duties in the war units as well as exceptional results achieved by the war units, it all reflected upon the strengthening of the morale. As regards the second anniversary of the formation of the staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica, which is now the command of the 8th operational group of Srebrenica as part of the 2nd Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina I commend the following soldiers. The command of the 283rd Light Brigade ready for inspection, commander Halilovic, Huso, reporting."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can stop here. Thank you. I would just like the Trial Chamber to know that we provided the translation booth with B/C/S text of these video clips. It was the inspection of 282 Brigade. We have the similar clips but we'll not show it to save the Court time of the other brigades from the 28th Division. I hope we will be able to do that through testimony of our investigator, Mr. Pero Mijatovic. The next video clip is the statement of B and H Prime Minister, Hasan Muratovic, in his speech on the session of B and H parliament held in August 1995, discussing the causes of the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: HE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The same situation applies to this clip. "Mr. Hasan Muratovic, Prime Minister, would like to speak. Dear Mr. Chairman, MPs, ladies and gentlemen. Let me briefly summarise a few things."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have identified Mr. Muratovic and I would ask to play the same video from 21 minutes, 47 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters were not provided with this part of the footage and the audio is too poor to decipher the speech itself. [Voiceover] "There is a question that should be clarified, whether Mr. Akashi had agreement with Mladic that people from Srebrenica should leave for Tuzla and that he would let them pass through. That needs to be explored. It was carried by the western press on several occasions and there were some theories coming from UN representatives that the people from Srebrenica should be let to pass peacefully through to Tuzla, therefore there are great chances that such an agreement existed. With some people from Srebrenica, I tried to talk about whether they had been told about such a possibility. Since there is a fact in existence and that is that our people were not shot at while they were coming out of the first encirclement of Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic however corroborated another submission of our Defence regarding intercept evidence. I would ask to play the same video from 16 minutes 5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Our army possesses a lot of audio tapes, tapes with executions on them, and about orders that the groups breaking through to Tuzla should be killed. We also have an intercept in which backhoe loaders and excavators were requested to dig mass graves."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This statement clearly corroborates our submission that B and H authorities are in possession of contemporaneous audio records of the intercept conversations. However, they refused to hand over such materials to this Tribunal, to avoid undermining of authenticity, reliabilities, and probative value of intercepts introduced in this and previous Srebrenica-related cases. We have challenged many conclusions by the Prosecution's military expert, Richard Butler through a number of witnesses, exhibits and testimony of our military -- and testimony of our military expert, we shall prove his erroneous interpretation of evidence related to the Srebrenica events in July 1995. Finally, we found that the background of the Srebrenica events in July 1995 is incomplete and misinterpreted. The first instance of such misinterpretation is the six strategic objectives of the Serbian people in B and H. We shall prove that it was nothing more than the plan made by European Union and its representative Portugal diplomat Cutileiro generously conceded to prevent the war in Bosnia. We shall prove that those objectives were not criminal but incorporated in Dayton Peace Agreement, document by which the war in Bosnia was ended. It will be clarified through our first witness, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. I'm aware that the background of the acts charged in the indictment is not main subject of this case. However, such information is very significant for comprehensive assessment of the events from the indictment. Because of that, it requires short but fair presentation of relevant background information. Accordingly, we shall address this issue as briefly as possible, not going into unnecessary analysis, polemics and details. I decided to present our view on the matters through short video clips from a number of DVDs from our exhibit list. I will not present this morning all these videos in their entirety in order to save the Court time. However all this video will be tendered into evidence. In presentation of the background, I submit that causes of the war in Bosnia could not be neglected. This complex and sensitive issue is summarised in the best way in the following clips from our exhibits from video, "The war which could be avoided." The film was divided in 32 chapters, each of them depicting the stage of war in former Yugoslavia. It explores the causes of war, the responsibility of main actors and contains the statements of many diplomats, politicians, journalists and military officers from United States, United Kingdom, Germany and former Yugoslavia. All details on authors of the film could be seen at the end of any chapter. Unfortunately, I'm just informed that the clips are not the same when presented at this video from this place, so I'm afraid we will not be able to show them right now. If the Trial Chamber let us, we will do that after some break, after break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a logistical problem in that we had planned other things precisely to coincide with the break taking place at 10.30 which we can't move now because it's too late. So we have a commitment at 10.30. How much time do you require to fix this thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I hope 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 10 to 15 minutes now so that you fix it, then we will continue, stop at 10.30 and then try to recover as much ground as we can as we go along, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.53 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, have you sorted out your technical problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I resolved them, and I apologise to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to apologise. These things happen, unfortunately. Yes, I recognise Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honour, sorry to interrupt, I just noticed Mr. Haynes isn't here. I don't know if Your Honours noticed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes is absent and in the meantime, I also wanted put on record that during the first part of the session, Mr. Mitchell, Christopher Mitchell, for the Prosecution also turned up. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because Mr. Sarapa is absent too today, unfortunately. All right. Mr. Pandurevic, we have a problem. Do you insist on your client's -- on your lawyer's presence? THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go ahead. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The video clips we shall see right now summarise our view on the background of Srebrenica events from the indictment. The first of it is the video of the war which could be avoided. We can play this video from 13 minutes 5 seconds. The clip we shall see right now presents a statements of the prominent British journalist, late Ms. Nora Beloff and the former U.S. Secretary of State, James Baker.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: " ... until there was an agreed arrangement it might take years or decades or perhaps might be impossible. Until then it had to be recognised these were the internationally recognised branches. If German and Austrian leaders still believe that Slovenia and Croatia could be separated from Yugoslavia without a wider war the Americans strongly believed otherwise. "Because we said if Yugoslavia does not break up peacefully, there is going to be one hell of a civil war. It nevertheless broke up non-peacefully, it broke up through the unilateral declaration of independence by Slovenia and Croatia and the seizing by these two country's republics of their border posts which was an act of force and which was an act that was in violation of the Helsinki principles, but the European powers and the United States ultimately recognised Slovenia and then Croatia and then Bosnia as independent countries, and admitted them to the United Nations. The real problem was that there was a unilateral declaration of independence and a use of force to gain that independence rather than a peaceful negotiation of independence which is the way it should have happened."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can stop here and we can move to 47, 16 seconds. It depicts the statements of the British diplomat, Lord Carrington, who was also involved in search for political solution of the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "This was a war that European leaders believed could have been avoided. The Bosnian Serbs until comparatively recently had been in the majority in Bosnia and then the Muslims who had a very much higher birth rate than the Serbs became the predominant, the majority population and this of course was something very hard for the Serbs to swallow and they made it abundantly plain very early on that they were not prepared to accept the situation in which there was an independent Bosnia under the constitution which then prevailed and indeed under the constitution which then prevailed it was illegal for Izetbegovic to declare independence because any constitution framed in that magnitude had to be agreed by all three parties. "Privately --"

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can stop here. The next clip from the same film is related to the Cutileiro Peace Plan for Bosnia. Please play from 50 minutes 55 seconds. [Videotape played] " ... politics of diplomacy then Secretary of State James Baker wrote that ambassador Zimmerman strongly advised him to recognition of Bosnia. Recognition of Bosnia, however, violated the most basic diplomatic norms. For a government to be recognised it must be in full control of its territory, it must have clearly established borders. It must also have a stable population. Not a single one of these essential conditions existed in Bosnia in February of 1992 when Zimmerman made his recommendations. US intelligence analysts predicted that recognition would lead to war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Haynes has entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like to say sorry to the Court and to Mr. Zivanovic, I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: " ... would be a serious mistake. "We did some different opinions in early 1992, as the Americans supported the recognition of Bosnia, whereas we, the Europeans, believed that we should first establish a framework for the whole region. "Basically the policymakers ignored the analysts and by late January, early February, US policy had come around to the view that we would recognise Bosnia and we wanted the Europeans to recognise Bosnia along with us so from mid-February on we were pushing the Europeans hard to recognise Bosnia and we were thinking about how we would do that and have the US recognise Croatia and Slovenia at the same time. With American support, recognition of the separate Bosnian state was now inevitable. Lord Carrington tried to avert disaster by appointing Portuguese president, Jose Cutileiro, to find common ground between the Serbs Muslims and Croats before an independent Bosnia was recognised. "I asked him to go to Sarajevo and Lisbon and have talks about the three parties in Bosnia to see whether or not an agreement could become -- could be reached. [Indiscernible] state, I mean a state, an independent Bosnian state within some sort of federal idea [indiscernible]. "The Bosnian Serbs, Croats, and Muslims all signed the pact known as the Lisbon agreement on March 18th, 1992. This set up a central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and three ethnic cantons on the model of Switzerland "It was the last chance, I think, to try and preserve Bosnia before the war broke out in Ernest. If the Lisbon plan had been adopted, British author and BBC journalist, Misha Glenny, wrote later the war in Bosnia probably would not have happened but two days after signing it following a meeting with American ambassador are Warren Zimmerman, Izetbegovic changed his minds and disavowed his signature. "Izetbegovic turned around and reneged as he's reneged on other things. "Zimmerman later acknowledged to David Binder of the New York Times that Izetbegovic had reluctantly signed the agreement to gain European recognition. More than a year after the blood shed began in Bosnia, Zimmerman also admitted that the Lisbon plan was not bad at all but recalls telling Izetbegovic if you don't like it, why sign it? "Zimmerman told Izetbegovic look, why don't you wait and see what the US can do for you meaning we will recognise you and then help you out so don't go ahead with the Lisbon agreement, don't accept the Cutileiro Plan and just hold out for some kind of unitary Bosnian state, so this is a major turning point in our diplomatic efforts. "The American administration made it quite clear that they thought that the proposal of Cutileiro were unacceptable. "With no agreement amongst the Muslims, Serbs and Croats and with all sides mobilised for war, the European community voted as the US insisted to recognise Bosnia on April 6th along with Slovenia and Croatia. This act, Roger Cohen of the New York Times later wrote was as close to criminal negligence as a diplomatic act could be. Indeed international recognition and the outbreak of the Bosnian war were simultaneous, the world put light to the fuse."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we can stop here. We shall also challenge the misinterpretation of the events in the spring 1992, when the Bosnian Serb military and paramilitary forces allegedly attacked and occupied cities, towns and villages including Bijeljina and Zvornik. The Prosecution disregarded the relevant fact that the Serbs in Bosnia held the 70 per cent of B and H land as a legal private property. I play the next clip corroborating this submission. These are well known western journalists, their names could be found in previous sequences of the film. I will take -- it will take less than a minute. Please play 1 hour 7 minutes 10 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: " ... trying to create balance of what the Bosnians were doing at the same time "The press would have us believe that the Serbs have seized the two-thirds of Bosnia. The fact is the Serbs had lived in that territory for 1500 years and the fact is they are farmers, and they are spread all over the landscape so they have always been on two-thirds of the landscape. "The statement that has become an absolute shade that the Serbs have taken over 70 per cent of Bosnia, again the underlying assumption is that there were no Serbs in Bosnia before the conflict started when in reality, much of the land of Bosnia was Serb land before the fighting ever began. But the implication is that the Serbs dropped in from some other planet and just took over nearly two-thirds of the country."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last clip from this video is the good instance of untrue information with inflated casualties, from -- it is related to another east Bosnian enclave Gorazde, which was in the area of responsibility of Drina Corps. Please play from 1 hour 43 minutes 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: " ... Western Herzegovina. Two months after the Markale Marketplace explosion, the Bosnian government would have its first success in getting NATO to intervene against Bosnian Serb targets near Gorazde. With help from an American military advisor, Muslim forces launched attacks against six Serbian villages around Gorazde. When Serbian forces responded, American television broadcasts portrayed fighting around Gorazde as if it were an unprovoked attack on a safe zone. "The Serbs punished Gorazde throughout the day. At one stage, shells were raining down at the rate of one every 20 seconds. "Shells are now dropping at random into the city centre, the hospital has taken direct hits on its roof. "There was a dramatic transmission from a hand radio operator supposedly based in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "US president Bill Clinton and Bosnian government vice-president, Ejup Ganic, urged UN Secretary-General, Boutros Boutros-Ghali to authorise air strikes against the Bosnian Serbs. NATO airplanes did indeed launch a limited air strike against Serbian targets. But further air strikes were called off by commander Michael Rose, who realised that Muslim forces had manipulated UN agencies with false casualty and damage reports. Instead of 2.000 people injured and 700 people killed, fewer than 200 people were injured. Instead of the hospital being destroyed, only one shell had passed through the roof. As he flew by helicopter into Gorazde following the fighting Rose was asked about US satellite reports that nearly every house in Gorazde was damaged. "Yes, practically every house in Gorazde has been damaged, but most of the damage to Gorazde was done in the fighting that had taken place some two years before when the Bosnian government forces drove the Serbs from this town and there were 12 and a half thousand Serbs at that time living there and they were all driven off. The way to distinguish a house that's been damaged by fighting where a shell has hit it and a house that's been damaged by ethnic cleansing is if its got no roof, no doors, no window frames, and nothing in the house at all and there are burn marks up in and bullets spread around the walls. That is the house that's been damaged by ethnic cleansing. A house that's been damaged by shelling has a shell hole in it, and there are still people trying to live in that building with their furniture because they've got no where else to go. That's something you can't see from satellite. And of course, at that time, the international image of what had happened in Gorazde very different from the reality. What was dangerous was that policies were going to be put together on both sides of the Atlantic, about what we should do in Gorazde but these policies had been put together on totally flawed information. "According to respected British military analyst, Jonathan Eyal, the ham radio operators whose live reports were carried on American television networks were not even based in Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it is my submission that most important and real background of the events from the indictment are atrocities perpetrated by Muslim forces in east Bosnia from the very on set of the war in the early spring 1992 until early July 1995 when the operation Krivaja was launched. We have gathered 25 videos illustrating the crimes committed in villages around Srebrenica, Bratunac and Vlasenica in order to illustrate it I'll play just a few clips although we shall tender all of them into evidence through our investigator, Mr. Pero Mijatovic, who provided them from the association of the former camp inmates of Republika Srpska. This material is not translated, so I tried to select the most relevant parts where the picture speaks everything. Please play the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "In addition to all the other civilian casualties, the elderly and the women, two children have also been killed. One was four and the other was nine or ten. They were siblings. "What was their names? Dragan Visnjic and Dragana, his sister. "How old were they? Dragan was four, and she was nine. "Hold on, hold on, wait. What? My little child, there you go, so that it holds like that. Her whole head is shattered."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. We can stop here. The second video clip shows the burial in Vlasenica of the victims murdered in late September 1992 in Cerska and Podravanje. This video is the second of three CDs illustrating the aftermath of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can stop here, thank you. And the last -- sorry, and the last of the video clips is recorded in May 1995, just a month before operation Krivaja 95 was launched. It depicts the massacre committed during and after the attack on Rupovo Brdo on May the 7th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can stop here, thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. We finished -- I have finished my opening statement and the Defence is now ready to call its first witness, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think before that we'll have the break. We will reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zivanovic, first of all I wish to thank you for having stuck to your estimated time for the statement, opening statement. Your first witness is Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning to you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are -- you have been summoned as a Defence witness by the Defence team for Mr. Popovic. You are aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are also familiar with our rules, one of which requires that before you start giving evidence, you are expected to make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth. Are you prepared to make that solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if could you give him the text and, Mr. Krajisnik, if you could read it out, please, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Please make yourself comfortable. There are a few things that I need to explain to you. Now, I take it that you have accepted to give evidence in this case after having been duly approached and asked to give evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, it's common knowledge that you have stood trial here, been found guilty and sentenced, and you have an appeal pending.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are two issues that arise out of that straight away, that I need to discuss very briefly with you. I know that in your proceedings, in your trial, and I think also in the appeal proceedings, you have decided to conduct your own Defence. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But these are different proceedings, in which you are only involved as a witness. According to our rules you still have a right to be assisted by counsel should you choose to ask for this or to request this. Has this been explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And have you asked to be assisted by counsel for the purpose of today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar has offered me the services of counsel, which I declined and decided to appear here without a counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you are confirming to us now that you don't require or you don't request the assistance of counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next thing I wanted to alert you to is a right that you have which is common to all witnesses here, and it applies to you because, for all intents and purposes, your case is still pending before the Appeals Chamber and your testimony here could potentially prejudice your case before the Appeals Chamber. So I need to alert you to a right that you have, to ask to be exempted from answering any question that may be put to you which, rather than incriminating you, could prejudice your appeal before the Appeals Chamber, but which could also perhaps expose you to criminal proceedings which could be incriminatory in your respect, in your regard. Now, in such instances, irrespective of who is asking you this question, you have a right to ask us, the Trial Chamber, to exempt you from answering such questions. We -- this right is not absolute. We can choose to grant such an exemption or we can choose to compel you to answer the question that is put to you. If we compel to you answer the question that is put to you, then the consequence is that if in answering that question you're truthful, whatever you say, and which could be incriminatory, will not be used against you in future proceedings before this Tribunal or elsewhere. Do you understand the import of this advisory that I am -- have just explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So there is one final thing that I need to communicate to you. You are currently in detention in the -- at the Detention Unit that we have here in Scheveningen, and I understand that you are being detained together with the accused in this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two of them. We need to place, to put in place an order for your segregation from these accused for the entire duration of your testimony here, after which, of course, the segregation will stop. So in these circumstances that you have confirmed, namely that you are currently being detained together with some accused in this trial, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, I am ordering that you be segregated from them during the course of your testimony. In case you fail to understand why, I will just explain to you that this is a standard procedure and it is directed at minimizing any risk of interactions that might have an effect on the reliability of a witness's testimony. So you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, but I would like to inform you about one thing, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Krajisnik. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The deputy head of the Detention Unit, Mr. Fraser, invited me on Thursday or Friday, I don't remember what day, to come to see him and ordered me to segregate myself from Mr. Beara and Mr. Borovcanin, and he established a regime. I spend all my days in my room whereas they are in their own rooms or in the common room, so we don't have any contact with each other, when we go for walks we never went together. I promised that I would obey the regime and they have done the same. He told me that he had already received an order to that effect from your Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The order hadn't been communicated. Of course, there were discussions and we wanted to know whether you were being detained with others or whether there was any segregation in place already as sometimes there is, and we also made clear that this would be forthcoming so that the Detention Unit commander or deputy commander would have advance notice of this and take the -- make the necessary preparations but that's about it. Anyway, the position is what it is. You're expected to last here giving evidence for a few days. I think we've come to the stage when Mr. Zivanovic can start. Mr. Zivanovic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to tell us for the record or to confirm your name. It is Momcilo Krajisnik, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there has been to be a break between your question and my answer and that's why I'm making a short pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're correct there. I would kindly ask you just briefly to give us your age and your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I was born on the 28th of January 1945, and I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I have a degree in economics. I have a masters degree in economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you also tell us about your professional background?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I worked before the first multi-party election in a company called Energoinvest. There was a member of the management board of one of the daughter companies. After the multi-party elections in 1990, I was elected a member of parliament and later on as the speaker of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. During the war, and before the war as well, from October 1991 until 1996, I was the speaker of the Assembly of the Serbian People, i.e. of Republika Srpska. After the Dayton Accords, I became a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that, for a year, I was in private business, and I've been here since 2000, a detainee in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let me start by asking you one thing that interests all of us here, something that would be the main topic of your testimony here. First of all, do you remember that you were presiding over a session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska that was held on the 12th of May 1992 in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at that session, a debate was held on the strategic goals of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally take the floor? Did you participate in the debate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I participated in the wording of the strategic goals before the very session. During the session itself, I participated partly in the discussion in order to summarise the debate and that was part of my engagement within the framework of the debate on the strategic goals, on the six strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, which means on the 12th of May 1992, when this session took place, had the armed conflicts already started in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Armed conflicts were already underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly about the atmosphere at that session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska? What was the mood of the assemblymen? What was their attitude towards their then political leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This was the first assembly session after the beginning of the war, or the armed conflict. I invited the assemblymen to Pale, but they couldn't come because the territorial communications had been interrupted. That's why we went to Belgrade, and from Belgrade we took a plane to Banja Luka, and we held the session there. The session -- the atmosphere was rather heated. Every assemblyman had brought the impression from their own area, some people had members of family killed, some lost their homes, some had been through ill-treatment. A lot of families had been separated so the overall situation at the session was very grave. And the assemblymen, to put it that way, were only prepared to say no. They were against everything. Their attitude was negative. They put up resistance to the danger that was imminent and to something that was new to them which was war, that nobody had been aware of before the war actually started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the development of the strategic goals that you referred to a moments ago. Can you tell me what the basis for the wording of the strategic goals was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In late April, between the 27th of April and 2nd or 3rd May, I can't recall the exact date now, a meeting was held as part of the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina in Lisbon, if I remember well. We achieved certain things there, we corrected the situation on the map, and some other matters, and we were quite optimistic that a settlement was looming there. We were told that through bilateral contacts, we should try and form an agreement on our respective views. After the conference, we went to Pale. We also went to Herzegovina in an attempt to formulate our next steps. On the 11th of May, a public announcement was made that the conference would be stopped. At that point, we presented our view as to the way in which the Serb delegates, the members of the Serb delegation of Republika Srpska, would develop their position for the negotiations. Through the six strategic goals, we defined all the views that we had previously advocated and suggested in the negotiations. These were some points that we believed we could achieve and upon which we believed we had the agreement of the two other sides, the Croat and Muslim, and the fourth party which was the international community. This was the formulation of our positions. We acted upon the suggestion that the Serb delegates, as representatives of the Serb people, were not in tune with the sentiment of the people when negotiating with the international community. This was a way of informing the international community and the public at large about our positions, since all the meetings and sessions we held were public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, the discussions about the strategic goals held at the various sessions were public, in other words, the members of the public could follow what was going on at the session through direct broadcasts or press coverage?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. All our sessions were public. The transcript of the sessions indicate that many people were present who were not MPs. For instance, I recall one Captain Galic having been presents there, and I'm sure that there were others. It was also open to the public at large. The room housing these sessions had a public gallery which was open to anyone who wanted to follow what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you the minutes from that particular assembly session. This is Prosecutor Exhibit P025. Do you recall this document by glancing at its cover page, although we can go through all the others? I believe you had an opportunity to look at the document during our proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The minutes and the transcript of the session was something that was known and discussed in my case too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who was it who spoke about these goals, who explained the goals to those present at the session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As part of the report on the current situation, Mr. Karadzic explained the six strategic goals to the MPs present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To refresh your memory, I will read out part of the minutes from the session held on the 12th of May 1992. That's page 12 in e-court. And you will have occasion to see what it's all about. That's the last paragraph. And it reads?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency the government the council for national security we formed have adopted strategic objective priorities of the Serb people or rather the strategic goals of the Serb people, the first of which is the separation from the other two ethnic communities, separation of the state. Can you please clarify what sort of separation is referred to here in respect of the -- or in relation to the other two ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This strategic goal was a demand that we had reformulated, and this was the position of the international community that within Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were able to have our own constituent unit which we could style as a state or any sort of unit. In order to set it up as a constituent unit, the Cutileiro Plan laid out the way in which it was to be done, by separating into different entities along an ethnic principle, where individual municipalities would be separated into separate constituent units and this would have been the way of achieving this goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The separation of the three ethnic communities, was it part and parcel of the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: These strategic goals were, in fact, reformulated Cutileiro principles which we believed we could achieve through negotiations, along with all the other aspects upon which we had the consensus of both the international community, on the one hand, and the Croat and Muslim sides on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you one other document, and ask you whether this is another part of Cutileiro Plan. This is Exhibit 1D1156. The first paragraph or chapter of the document under A reads that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be a state composed of three constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographic and other criteria. Do you recognise these principles from the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now turn to the next page, or, rather, page 3 of the document where, under E, the following is stated, and this is true for both of the versions, that a working group will be established in order to define the territory of the constituent units based on national principles, and taking into account economic, geographical and other criteria. Do you recall this other principle from the Cutileiro Plan as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a map that goes with this plan, which indicates the makeup of the population as it was in the previous years. I will not be asking you about these -- the map, but did there exist a map that was produced by representatives of the international community led by Mr. Cutileiro?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at Exhibit 1159. 1D1159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Seems to be some problem with that because we can't find it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the map can be placed on the ELMO and the witness can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's readily available, I think that would be a good suggestion, but for the future, check the reference number because it doesn't seem to tally. Yes, your question, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can see the map, can you please confirm for us that this is indeed the map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. This is the map that was produced following the meeting in early May 1992 and I'm referring to the meeting in Lisbon. I believe it was held in Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain how this meeting came about, or, rather, how this idea came about of negotiating with the help of the European Community or, rather, its representative, Mr. Cutileiro?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Once the referendum on independence was scheduled in Bosnia, which was in late January 1992, we received an initiative document to the effect that a representative of the international community would come with a proposal that would form a compromise between our option, whereby we wanted -- we, I mean the Serb side -- to keep Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia, and the option espoused by the Muslim and Croat sides, whereby Bosnia-Herzegovina should become a state independent of Yugoslavia. They were testing us to see whether we were prepared to have Bosnia and Herzegovina recognised as an independent country and having Bosnia-Herzegovina cantonalized where we would have our own cantons or regions. We were told that the principle would be the majority of different ethnic groups in different parts of the country. The first mediator in that effort was the leadership of Serbia, specifically Mr. Milosevic. Later on, Mr. Cutileiro also showed up and presented these principles and that was how the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina commenced at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the commencement of the conference, was a plebiscite held at which the Serb people were given an opportunity to state whether they wanted an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina or some other alternative?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. It was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what the upshot of that was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: By absolute majority, over 90 per cent of the population, of the Serb population, and this included also a small percentage of Bosnians, Muslims, that's to say and Croats, and a small percentage of those who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs, these members of the population opted to stay within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly that consenting to the Cutileiro Plan would mean giving up the decision or the results of the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a significant concession that the Serbian side made at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That is correct, and I wish to explain, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: On the 15th of October, against the constitution, the Muslim and Croatian side came up with a memorandum establishing a platform concerning the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serbian MPs vetoed it, and we were told then that we did not have the right to refuse an independent Bosnia on behalf of the Serbian people because the other side claimed that the Serbian people were divided and that there were many of them who were in favour of the independent Bosnia. We organised a referendum in order to establish how and what it is that the Serbian people want and whether they wanted a decision they had adopted. It was done in order to feel the pulse of the people. When we said that we would accept independent Bosnia, but regionalized, we wanted to offer a compromise solution which, again, required a referendum on the part of all citizens in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the Serbian people. We would not -- we did not play it upon the Serbian people, so to say, but our wish was to feel the pulse of the public. When I say, "We," I meant the negotiating team. We were told either you accept a compromise or you lose everything, and we were in favour of a compromise. We stood by those principles throughout the negotiations, until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the Cutileiro Plan and according to the strategic goals you set up, was it envisaged that within those predominantly ethnic -- uni-ethnic entities there would be space for people of other ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Certainly. In no way did we strive for any movements of population. That was completely excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to read to you the third strategic goal. I will not go through all six of them since they are not overly relevant for the case here. However, I would move to the third goal now. It reads, "The third strategic goal is to establish a corridor in the Drina River valley, that is eliminate the Drina as a border separating the two worlds." Please clarify the third strategic goal, given that there is a mention of the Drina River valley and a corridor there as well as the border between the two worlds. Firstly, please explain whether the corridor and the borders referred to were two separate issues or one and the same?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Before the international community was included in early 1992, we had had frequent contacts of the three sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I represented Bosnia and Herzegovina in the negotiating team when negotiating with Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro and other republics. During those negotiations with the Muslim side, we put forth our reasons as to why we cannot accept an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina and us being separated from our home land, that is Serbia, and why it is that we cannot accept that a proper, so to say, border be set up along the Drina. There was the same position that the Croatian side had. As was confirmed later, a solution came up, put forth by the Muslim side. They said, "We don't have to have a border with border posts and requiring people to move about with passports. Those borders have to be permeable, for example if one wants to go from Bosnia to Serbia, one shouldn't need a passport." And that applied to Croatia as well. Mr. Izetbegovic during the first congress of his party, stated that clearly. I think it was in December 1991, when he said no matter what the solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina is going to be, there will be no border at the Drina River, it will not require having a passport. And in that way, that represented a relief, psychologically speaking, to our side. As you will see in the negotiations and in the Dayton agreements as well as the Cutileiro Plan, special links were envisaged between the entity of Republika Srpska with the other so-called neighbouring states. Of course, the federation enjoyed the equal status. That was primarily upon our request although the Muslim side was to use it as well because there were Muslims in Serbia as well as the Croatian side in Bosnia because the neighbouring state of Croatia was nearby. That was the reason why we inserted this goal as such. As for the corridor, if you study Mr. Karadzic's presentation or his speech, he said, "We can now see enclaves in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But the corridor is there to link up our different territories. As one of our priorities we stated that we wanted links among the different parts of our constituent unit. Mr. Cutileiro said the following: These are the principles and as for the corridors and the rest, you have the right to agree on them with the other side, even if it requires an exchange of territory. That is why we introduced a corridor between the southernmost part of our ethnic territories which is southern Herzegovina and Romanija as well as Semberija and this includes the other corridor which however was not part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was Mr. Alija Izetbegovic's idea. Please have a look at Exhibit 1105. It is 1D1105. This is Mr. Izetbegovic's speech during the first congress of his party, the Party of Democratic Action. Please have a look at page 2, its ultimate paragraph. Mr. Izetbegovic says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the official translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "In such a situation, a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina in a free community of nations is the only guarantee of dignified and free -- of a dignified and free life, not only for the Muslim people but for the Serbs and Croats as well. Given the ethnic makeup, such a Bosnia-Herzegovina needs to develop special relations on both -- with both Serbia and Croatia. Irrespectively of their mutual links, that is the links between those two independent states. We believe that needs to be resolved, the Serbs should not have a feeling that they are divided from Serbia with a state border. The same applies for Croatians. Therefore, no passports for the Serbs along the Drina or the Croats along the Una River." Does this sentence accurately reflect what Mr. Izetbegovic said concerning the future borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic fairly stated what he had stated during the negotiations. This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back again to the principles of the Cutileiro Plan. It is 1D1156. We've already seen that. Page 2. Page 2, please. In both versions, in the English it spills over to page 3. It is chapter D. Have a look at the last sentence. It reads, "A constituent unit may establish and preserve links with other republics and states provided that they are in keeping with inviolability of Bosnia-Herzegovina as such." Does this correspond to the Cutileiro Plan principles?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, and they were later termed special parallel links or relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The sentences we quoted from Mr. Izetbegovic's speech, as well as this particular sentence taken out of the outlines of the plan concerning the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is the same thing that you envisaged as part of one of your strategic goals of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. However, in the goals, it was reformulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But the essence of it is the same?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may have a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I read the entire minutes of the assembly session of the 12th of May 1992. However, I did not see any mention of any decision being adopted according to the strategic goals. I did not see that there was a vote of acceptance or anything of that sort. Can you tell me whether a decision was made at the session, a formal legally binding decision, or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: There was no decision made and there was no vote on the strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it because the presentation of the strategic goals was there merely to acquaint the MPs with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've been holding back but there has been several leading questions and now I'm going to start to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you're put on notice Mr. Zivanovic, and you need to adjust your style of questioning accordingly. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what were the reasons that no decision was made concerning the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The strategic goals were there as a type of information, the goal of which to acquaint the MPs with what the delegation's position was at the negotiations. It could have happened that there was a vote on the objectives because that was the first session, and we were under a lot of pressure and the agenda was extensive. However, it did not happen because it wasn't our goal to oblige anyone by adopting any decisions. Our goal was to continue with the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I had occasion to see, and I showed to you, an Official Gazette of Republika Srpska. It's edition of the 26th of November 1993, in which the strategic goals were published in the form of a decision. Please explain how that came about.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I can respond in two ways, depending on the decision of the Appeals Chamber -- sorry, Trial Chamber, because I keep having the Appeals Chamber in mind. I can tell you what I recall, and I can tell you what is it that I found out during my appeal proceedings, and something I discovered by chance since our last meeting on Friday. It has to do with the publication of this decision. And I can now tell you what it is that I recall and it is up to you whether you wish to hear the other two pieces of information, because these represent two missing links in a chain of which I wasn't aware at the time of my testimony. I recalled what was happening with the strategic goals up until the session. I know why we presented them. However, I had no knowledge of them being published. I had forgotten that, and only when I reviewed the documentation here, I conducted different investigations and I came up with certain results. This is what I recall, and this was part of my testimony. When testifying in my case, I based it on that. I testified on what I remembered, and I was unable to view the whole background and the situation. This is what I can recall off the cuff. I never, at the time, knew that the strategic goals had been published. I may have forgotten, but it is only now that I'm filling in the gaps in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm not going to insist on you belabouring your answer with that respect. However, we heard an explanation here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, just to clarify, if I can i I'm not sure it's clear from the answer, what time the witness was referring to when he said, "I never at that time knew that the strategic goals had been published." Is that a reference to the time he testified in his trial which was the way it appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you understand -- Mr. Krajisnik, do you understand what Mr. Nicholls' concern is? Yes? Can you enlighten us on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, if my memory serves me correctly, up to the moment when I arrived here in the Detention Unit, I don't remember ever having been aware of the strategic goals being published. Let me put it this way: I did not have them available to me because I was not aware of them. I only knew that they were discussed at the assembly meeting, and I knew that they were never voted upon. This is what I meant when I provided my answer to Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, does that satisfy your concern? Yeah, okay. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we've had a witness here, actually an expert witness, who told us that the strategic goals had not been published for a long time because they would have revealed a criminal act, that that's the reason why these goals were not published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, stop, stop. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we have the reference, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zivanovic? Who were you referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in one part of testimony of Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Butler. I imagined so but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say right now what the part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This isn't how it shouldn't be. If you're prepared all the time to give a specific reference if you're referring to a particular part of someone else's testimony. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just got the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 19672 until 675 -- 674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you will check while we proceed. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, do you wish Mr. Zivanovic to repeat his question? Or do you still have a memory of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered that what the expert witness said was not correct, and I can prove that by documents that I have discovered in the meantime, since Friday, actually, on Saturday, when I was preparing myself for this testimony, I came across some documents, and I can show you how the decision was taken and why the decision was only published on the 25th of November 1993. I can give you the whole course of the process leading to the publication of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, from the moment when the debate on the six strategic goals took place at the National Assembly session in May 1992 and further on, did the political leadership of the Republika Srpska kept on insisting on these goals in the negotiations with the other parties and in the negotiations that were being carried out under the auspices of the international community?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just again, it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't believe so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have no doubt in our mind, not even the least possible doubt, that of course this is a leading question, so please be kind enough to rephrase it, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, was the international community ever informed about these strategic goals from 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to these strategic goals, were they the foundation for striking some future deals and concluding some negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
