utterances.text: Some 15 minutes ago, I said that based on those principles, we conducted all of our negotiations up to the Dayton Accords which means that we advocated these goals and we insisted on these goals being implemented during the negotiations because they were the reflection of what had been agreed by the four sides at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as for these strategic goals, were they incorporated and to what extent in the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As for the strategic goals that we advocated during the negotiations, all we got was Republika Srpska and the corridors. We did not get the part of Sarajevo that we had agreed upon. We did not get access to the sea because the proposal that was adopted by the Dayton Accords was not signed and was not attached to the final version of the Dayton Accords. In my view, it was not the goal for them to be realised. It was the goal to work on those and to achieve Republika Srpska and to achieve an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the other hand, and to lay down a foundation for independent Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Don't wish to interrupt, Your Honour, but I found the portion of the transcript my friend referred to. For the record what Mr. Butler said, on page 19764 in answer to a question, answer: My understanding is that while the actual strategic objectives were articulated in May 1992 for whatever reason the government of Republika Srpska did not decide to publish those in their own Official Gazette until 1993. I don't know the exact reason why they elected to do that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which does not really correspond with what you suggested to the witness, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll double check it. Sorry. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's go ahead. It corresponds more with what the witness himself said. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you this: When it comes to the strategic goal referring to the borders between the two worlds, as it is stated therein, was that ever realised?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, if we got an internal border between Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was translated into us having separated ourselves or ended up with a regionalization or cantonization. This is the -- where the internal borders were drawn between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the other borders that are referred to in strategic goals as borders between the two world, in other words between Bosnia-Herzegovina on the one side and Serbia and Croatia on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, this is the interpretation that we have mentioned and we have seen which was articulated by Mr. Izetbegovic, and this is not to have a feeling of borders between the two worlds, meaning between Republika Srpska, i.e. Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbia. However, he was talking about the psychological border between the Serbs on the one side of the Drina and the other side of the Drina because that was the problem and that was the reason why special links were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please also tell me whether that goal has ever been realised?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina today there are no passports to be flashed at the Drina River. You can cross the Drina River with your personal ID. There is a border, but you don't need a passport to cross that border. It is well known that Bosnia-Herzegovina is on one bank, on the other there is Serbia, and all the people can cross without any visa, without any special requests, which is beneficial for both the citizens of Serbia as well as for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, this does not apply only to Serbs but to all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all citizens of Serbia and the same situation is on the Una, on the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia which means that all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina can cross freely into Croatia which is an independent site on the other bank of the river Una.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. That will be all. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I see Mr. Meek and Madam Fauveau conversing. You both asked to cross-examine Mr. Krajisnik. I saw your filing this morning, Mr. Meek. Who is going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. At this time we have no questions on cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Meek. Then let's go round. Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours at this moment I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow us a 20-minute break in order to consult with your clients because the information in chief has been curtailed significantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough, Madam Nikolic. In the meantime, before we break, can I have an indication as to who else wishes to cross-examine? I know that you wish, Madam Fauveau, if you still wish to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to consult my client, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Let's have a -- would 25 minutes be enough for you? Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. In the meantime, should we find ourselves surprised a second time today, are you in a position to start with your cross-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. A 25-minute break. --- Break taken at 12.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So as you noticed, we have Judge Prost missing. She is on official business and she will be away the rest of the sitting today and also tomorrow. She'll be back with us on Wednesday, when we will be sitting in the afternoon and not in the morning. So that means we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, okay? Mr. Meek, you still don't wish to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. At this time we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Nikolic or Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will have a very short cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My name is Stephane Bourgon, and I am counsel in these proceedings on behalf of Drago Nikolic. My cross-examination will be rather short. I only have a couple of questions for you. The first one being the following: Based on your testimony and the answers you gave to my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic, it would appear to me that the Republika Srpska government and assembly did everything that could possibly be done in order to avoid the war in Bosnia. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. My view is that you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my second question, Mr. Krajisnik, is: Looking back at your personal role and involvement as the president of the Republika Srpska Assembly during the war in Bosnia, and I refer to the period from 1992 to 1996, what knowledge do you have, if any, of the existence of a policy within the Republika Srpska government, and/or assembly, to get rid of the Muslim or Croat population living in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No, there did not exist such a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Krajisnik, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As we already indicated, we will have no cross-examination of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm that with you. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, you said a while ago, page 47, that you could explain why the decision to publish the strategic objectives had been taken only the 25th of November 1993. Could you indeed tell us why this decision to publish these strategic objectives was taken practically a year and a half after the assembly of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could you please read out exactly what I said? Because I'm afraid that it might have been mistranslated. I didn't say that I could explain why the decision was taken at the time but why it was published at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed there is a problem of interpretation. This is precisely the question I wanted to ask. Could you explain why the decision to publish the strategic objectives was taken only in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would like to refrain from correcting you. Rather I shall explain what you're most probably interested in. I said that I could explain the course of the events that I explained in my appeals brief and what I was able to ascertain in the documents that I was perusing since Friday. And I can tell you why there was this error committed in the publication of the decision concerning the six strategic goals. If you're interested I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you say briefly why this decision was published in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Here is my answer. Before I came across the relevant documents, I was not able to remember why it was published at a later date. What I will say now has to do with the documents that I came by during my appeal and it will be based on the documents that I was able to peruse whilst I was preparing to testify for Mr. Zivanovic. First of all, on the 9th of June 1992, at the session which was of a consultative character, the following decision was taken: That the strategic goals and the map of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina be published and that they be sent to the international community. This was the penultimate item of the agenda of the extended meeting of the Presidency. It can be easily located, and I have the relevant minutes here with me. After that, an enactment was developed, namely conclusions which explicitly state what Mr. Karadzic stated at the meeting held on the 12th of May 1992, or rather at the session held on that date. This differs from the text of the decision as published later, and I have that particular document as well. I had signed it. Next, and this is something that I'm speculating about, it wasn't clear whether it was decided whether it should be published in the Official Gazette or whether it should simply be published provided to the public. Somebody corrected the minutes in their own hand and this was something that I was able to find out on Saturday. I can also explain why it was that I only realised this last Saturday and not before. In this way, the conclusions were formulated in the form in which the decision was in fact published on the 25th of February 199-- 25th of October 1993. The decision was ultimately typed out, but you can see that at the very session, the decision did not state that the strategic goals should be published in the Official Gazette. It was merely said that it would be made public because one cannot publish the map in the Official Gazette. That's why I gather that the intention was simply to have the decision known in -- to the public rather than publish it in the Official Gazette. Let me just give you an aside. Orders and binding mandatory documentation is published in the Official Gazette. One would not publish conclusions in the Official Gazette. For that reason, the decision was not published in the Official Gazette. Now we come to the year 1993. We had it in the archives but it had not been published in the Official Gazette. Next, in the month of October of 1993, a report on the four years work of the assembly of the Republika Srpska was being prepared. A lawyer came to my office, and he was describing to me the events of the four years that would be included in the report and he came across that decision. And he made a note in which he said the decision was not registered anywhere in the Republika Srpska documentation or signed. At that point, I must have signed the decision because it bears my signature and it was forwarded for publication. This report, which was published in October of 1993 makes reference to the fact that the assembly had debated or adopted strategic goals, and I'm referring to the assembly meeting of the 12th of May 1992. I have all the paper work that I have referred to. I have it here. I can show it to you. Now, why did I not give this to Mr. Zivanovic? I had not been aware of the corrections or the minutes that were made while I was testifying. I only learned about this during my appeal because my investigators gave me numerous documents. The decision had been published in ten copies or more, and enclosed with it was the transcript from the assembly meeting complete with the two documents I mentioned, the two conclusions. It was on the basis of these documents that I was able to make the necessary links that I lacked, pointing to the reason why the decision was not published in 1992 but rather in 1993. Now, on the 20th of June 1992, the decision had gone through the protocol. It was entered into the protocol book or the logbook, and we have that particular logbook dating back from 1992. All the documents were entered under the 12th of May whereas this particular decision was entered into the logbook under the date of the 20th of July. This is the extent of the information I was able to come by, and that I wished to convey to the Trial Chamber in order to try and explain why the events took this course, and this is the extent of the knowledge that I referred to while I was testifying a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen the transcript as yet. All right. Thank you. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Which means, Mr. Nicholls. Now, Mr. Zivanovic had estimated nine to ten -- actually nine hours for the examination-in-chief of this witness, and -- but I have also another document which says six hours. How long do you anticipate your cross-examination will last or will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours I anticipate I will go into tomorrow. I'll have to go through the transcript tonight. I think I will be able to cut it down somewhat, but I will, I think, have a few hours. There is some new information here that I frankly don't completely understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean by a few hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I can do it probably in less than my original estimate. Perhaps two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay but do you anticipate you will need the whole of tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Which means you need to have your next witness available tomorrow, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which means other colleagues are going to stand up and say they are not yet prepared. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this witness is very important for the Defence of Popovic. He arrived only this morning. He will have a session, a proofing session, and if we begin tomorrow, we will have no possibility to have this witness before he begins. And also, this is the same for other colleagues of the Defence. This puts us in an impossible situation because we still haven't received the list of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're referring to Lazic, I take it? Your next witness will be Miljenko Lazic or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct. So what's the problem with that, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was a problem of interpretation. It's also for Beara and Popovic Defence and Miletic, so the Defence of Popovic will have an opportunity to have a proofing session today with the witness, but the Beara Defence and Miletic Defence will not have this possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but we can't go on like this. That's why when we had the Pre-Defence Conference I said, and I repeated it, I don't know how many times, that you need to organise yourselves. We are not here to waste time. Tomorrow we start with Lazic, and you will need to tell us beforehand, Mr. Zivanovic, whether you will still intend to utilise the 17.5 hours that you had indicated or whether you will do as you did today, cut down from nine hours to one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 17.5 hours is time estimated for my examination of my colleagues and cross-examination. My examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Including everyone? Tomorrow you will start with Lazic and then we will try to organise yourselves in a way which if you need to go last you will go last and similarly if the Beara team needs more time, we will make arrangements accordingly, but we start with Lazic tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into closed session -- private session, previously, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, which also means basically, ladies and gentlemen, that I need to repeat to you that we need to organise ourselves or rather you need to organise yourselves accordingly. We have our own problems. When this happens we have to liaise with our staff because things or events drop on us and we have to react accordingly. So as I take it, you may find yourself -- when I say you, it could be whoever, I don't know who will be in charge of Lazic -- that you may find yourself needing to cross-examine this witness even earlier than you may have anticipated. Which then leads me to another problem. On paper, we were looking at this week and a good part of next week almost entirely devoted to Krajisnik and Lazic. It may well turn out to be different. Don't bring us to the situation, Mr. Zivanovic, when we approach one of the days towards the end of this week with no witnesses here, present here, in The Hague to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we bring our -- we do our best to bring the next witnesses as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Otherwise, I can guarantee you full cooperation from the Trial Chamber, but don't put us in an impossible position because we have responsibilities of our own and accountability of our own. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, you can start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to say very briefly Your Honours as you recognised it can create problems for us as well in our scheduling and so that if -- I also understand that estimates change but if we could be informed as soon as possible that direct is going to be cut by 75 per cent that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it would be helpful not only to you but -- and to the other Defence teams, but definitely also to the Trial Chamber. And our staff. Because we usually have detailed one member of the staff to examine and report back to us on each witness that is anticipated. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Bourgon briefly started talking about your role, the role that you played, during the time that you were speaker of the Republika Srpska Assembly. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he asked you, I don't have it on my screen but to confirm that it was never the purpose to, paraphrasing, chase other ethnicities out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit, briefly, about your role in that conflict. You've been convicted in this building of crimes against humanity, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've been convicted of murder or extermination for approximately 3.000 human beings, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I haven't come here to testify about my role but rather of the six strategic goals or should I say of two of those. That's why I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to allow me not to answer these questions. If we may focus on the central issues for which I was called to appear here. I would not wish to be misunderstood or I would not wish my statements to be abused for the purposes of my appeal. That is a separate case that I will be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm going briefly to some questions that go directly to the witness's credibility. These are simply facts I wish to put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. If we need to explain to the witness the correct position at law, we will do so but in the meantime I think you can move safely to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were also found guilty, criminally responsible, for the forcible removal of more than 100.000 Muslims and Croats, correct? That's what your trial judgement says in paragraph 1144.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I was convicted for ethnic cleansing and persecutions, and I don't know what number that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And since Mr. Bourgon brought up your role, in assessing your responsibility, the Trial Chamber found that your involvement in your position was crucial to the commission of the crimes charged in the Prosecution's indictment, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object to this question because it goes to analyse the judgement in the -- another case, in the case of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Goes directly to his credibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a direct question which is very simple to answer, if the witness is au courant or knows the details of the judgement that was rendered against him. The question is a very simple one, whether he agrees the fact that the Trial Chamber that decided his case found that his involvement and his position was crucial to the commission of the crimes charged in the Prosecution indictment. It's not whether he believes it was so or not or whether he agrees with the decision of the Trial Chamber but whether the Trial Chamber actually did decide in that manner, in that -- so, Mr. Krajisnik, from your recollection of the judgement, final judgement, of the Trial Chamber, do you agree that the Trial Chamber found in your respect that your involvement was crucial to the commission of the crimes charged in the Prosecution's indictment in your case? Whether you agree with the finding is another matter. We are not asking you to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber found that I was one of the key individuals in the joint criminal enterprise, which had as its goal the expulsion of the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That should suffice. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Last question on this topic. You testified in your case for 40 days, at paragraph 888 of the judgement, in a special section on your credibility, the Trial Chamber found that you were of "very low credibility." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I want to go now to the 16th Assembly session which you've discussed. As president of the assembly, you chaired that session, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you chaired, correct, virtually I think all but one sessions of the RS Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I believe that that's correct. There were meetings that I left early on but I definitely participated in them. So my answer is I was present at all the sessions but one, though I may have left some of them early on so I might have been present throughout or in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we have P25 up, please? That is the 16th Assembly session. While we are waiting for that to come up, at this same assembly session you recall the army of the -- what would become called the VRS was established formally?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Ratko Mladic was appointed commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go to the English, page 13, it's the -- actually, it's 13 in both, I believe. And I don't know if anybody has the English up. I don't. If anybody needs it. Okay. In any event I just want to go over the way Karadzic enunciated the first strategic goal. I think my friend read the first part. I want to continue. The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities, separations of states. And then he continued: "Separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us. And who would continue with such practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Top of the page, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I haven't gotten to my question yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You recall Karadzic saying that at the session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I don't recall saying -- I don't recall him saying that but I believe his submission was along these lines. I don't remember his exact words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can see it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- clearly he's talking about the separation of peoples.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Not about the separation of peoples. I can explain to you why he used such terms, because I knew the background, and I knew what his intention was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, your answer then is no, it is not about separation of people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go quickly now to the 42nd assembly session, 65 ter number 3305, page 1 in the English, page 71 in the B/C/S. Previously had a little difficulty getting this correctly into e-court, so I hope it comes up now. This is -- excuse me. Sorry, this is the 18th and 19th of July 1994. Page 71 of the B/C/S. And it should be on numbered page 1 in the English. The part I want you to focus on is as follows: "We know for sure that we have to give something up."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is it, roughly, in the page, top, first half, second half? Upper, lower half? What?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of page 71, excuse me, and the top of page 72 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In English. I'm not bothered about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the English, it's in the middle paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's correctly up on the screen now in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But for the witness we need to go to the next page, 71, as I said. I'll read it out while we are waiting and if you need to read it on the screen, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic said at this session: "We know for sure we have to give something up. That is clear beyond a shadow of a doubt. If we wish to achieve our primary strategic aim which is to get rid of the enemies in our house, the Croats and Muslims, and not to be in the same state with them any more." Again, this is Dr. Karadzic talking about not being in the same state with persons of other ethnicities, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The interpretation should differ. Had we explained it a moment ago it would have been clear now. One needs to know what the basis, the background, of this discussion was. As far as I can recall it had to do with the plan put forth at the assembly. Had I been able to see the agenda I would have been able to tell you exactly what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And very briefly, if we can have P02755 up on the screen, this is the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska from the 26th of November 1993. Publication on the decision on the strategic objectives for the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And let me just read in the preamble which is under the number 386, "At its session held on 12 May 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted the following decision." And then it lists the six strategic objectives. Very briefly, just to be clear we hadn't seen this yet in the direct, this publication refers to exactly the same 12 -- same strategic objectives enunciated in the 12th May session in Banja Luka, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It is not correct. These strategics differ from those formulated by Mr. Karadzic and differ from the conclusions I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the 16th Assembly session and see what was spoken of there. Now, Bosanska Krupa was one of the municipalities of the ARK, Autonomous Region of Krajina, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No. Not at first, because only one of its parts was a part of the ARK. I don't know when it became a part of the ARK. Perhaps even after the end of the war. In any way, it didn't follow the same procedure that the other municipalities with the predominant Serb majority did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a municipality west of Banja Luka, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's -- parts of it at least are along the Una River, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That municipality is on both sides of the Una.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, a man you know, Miroslav Vjestica, was a member of the RS Assembly from Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He attended the 16th Assembly session in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He spoke at that assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I see you remember, but anyway, let's go over what Mr. Vijestica said. That's again 16th Assembly session which is P25, go to page 25 of the English, beginning on page 21 at the bottom, I guess, of the B/C/S. Maybe on page 22 of the B/C/S, but what I still have on my screen is the prior assembly session. Or later assembly session. That's right. Thank you. Let me go through a little bit about what Mr. Vijestica said. This will take a moment, Your Honour, for me to read this. I want to put it in. "Mr. President,' steamed people's deputies, members of the Presidency, dear guests, I will briefly tell you, inform you, of the situation in the theatre of war in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa." And then he talks about how he will try to be brief. He begins immediately talking about the six strategic goals which he has heard that day on 12th May in Banja Luka. "I give my full consent to all the strategic goals that have been proposed, but I would like to note that individuals must be appointed and operationalized who shall be responsible for carrying out the activities related to each individual goal. Because I do not believe it is sufficient to declare here that the Sava River is our border and then learn, in the course of the day, that Bosanski Brod has fallen and that there are no more Serbs there and so on." And he continues a little bit further down. "What have we done in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa? I must tell you to remind you all that Serbs compromise only 24 per cent of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa. There are 14.500 of us and there are 47.000 Muslims. As our president has said, we, in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa, did not want the war but we were forced into it." And for a little bit further down, he says: "For a year and a half we have been preparing for war in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa because we knew that there would be war and that it could not be avoided." And then he continues and begins to talk about what is going on now, on the ground, in Krupa. "Thank God we did get to our borders because that's how we had envisaged them and drawn them and you people's deputies know well that the right bank of the Una River would be our border and that the right bank of the Una River must be the border after all, the natural border of the Serbian Republic of B H." And it continues. "That was what we kept claiming and that was why we did get to the right bank of the Una River. This is where we stopped, where we dug in. We have mined the right bank. We have mined the iron bridge, the wooden one, we have blown up, and now we are preparing for Bosanska Otoka. God willing, in two to three days we shall mine the bridge in Bosanska Otoka connecting it with Bosanski Novi. This will be done, I guarantee it. What are our adversaries doing? At the moment, they are all in Cazin Krajina. On the right bank of the Una River, there are no more Muslims in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa. All the enclaves that were there, Rapusa, Veliki, Vrbovik, Ostroznica, Babic, Muslim Jasenica and Zavir, we have evacuated them. So there will be none there for the duration of war operations. Will they have a place to return to? I think it is unlikely, after our president told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una River was the border." He continues on the next page to discuss the disarming which is taking place by the SDS in Bosanski Novi, and Sanski Most. And he says, "I think the Muslims will be disarmed there as well." Now, your response as the next speaker to that speech by Mr. Vijestica, which is on page 22 of the B/C/S and page 26 of the English, is, "Thank you." And then you tell who is going to speak next. Mr. Vijestica told you in that session about what was happening in Bosanska Krupa, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. He told you, perhaps you knew this at the time, that only 24 per cent of the population was Serb, right? That was in his speech to you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, he said 24 per cent. I believe he said that. That's when he stated the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he told you what had happened in his municipality to the Muslim population, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Vijestica said what you read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a misstatement. He addressed to the assembly not to the witness personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the witness was included and he was chairing. So what difference? Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, this is a misinterpretation because Mr. Vijestica was only talking about the right bank of the Una River, and he never mentioned the left bank of the Una river whereas earlier we heard something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... totally inappropriate objection. That is a totally inappropriate objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. Let's proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He told you, and everyone else present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to go into this because when you are in a meeting you address the chair in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That his understanding after Mr. Karadzic's enunciation of the strategic goals, was that the Muslims would not be allowed to return. That's what he said, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Please, if you wanted the truth, then you should have shown us his interview to the Prosecutor's Office. It was all explained by Mr. Vijestica. I read that interview, and I can offer you my interpretation. I can tell you what it was that I thought he was talking about. There is the OTP interview in which he explained it all. Let us have a look at the interview, and you'll see what it is that he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is not my question. My question is just that it's correct what we've got written down here, he said that his understanding was that the Muslims would not be allowed to return. That's what he said at the assembly session, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And he explained it in his interview to you, as to what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So the answer to my question is yes, and now you're referring to an interview. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, I think I'm being prevented from stating my answer in full and my answer is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, I believe that the Prosecutor should not say that the Muslims were not able to come back. Where exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no idea what the objection is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't either. It's probably that there is no specificity as to where exactly they would not be able to return. I think we can move on to your next question, Mr. Nicholls. Otherwise we are going to go into the argument what the right bank of the Una River meant, whether it was restricted to that part relating to Bosanska Krupa or whether it extended to other sections. Let's move to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If I can just say for the record I think it's pretty clear for from the text it says the Muslims have been evacuated from these enclaves in our municipality, they won't be able to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered the question. Let's move, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to talk now, in the time we have left today, about some events shortly after the 16th Assembly session. All right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we could have 65 ter 3252, please? This is from the first page in both languages. This is a first Partizan Brigade command document from the 12th of June 2006. Excuse me, that's not correct, the 14th of May 1992. Of a meeting which took place amongst members of presidents of various Serbian municipalities in the ARK area and some military commanders. We can see the agenda is number 1, review of the military and political situation in the municipalities. Number 3, messages from the meeting of the armed forces of Serbian Krajina and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Banja Luka on 12 May 1992. Present at this meeting, I'll go through some of them, commander of the 30th Partizan Division, Colonel Stanislav Galic; commander of the 6th Partizan Brigade, Colonel Branko Basara, who was then the 6th Krajina brigade commander later. Chief of the 30th Division, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Kokovic, and the commander of the TO for Kljuc, Major Bosko Lukic; president of Kljuc municipality, Jovo Banac and others. If we go now to page 3, it's page 3 in both languages, the president of the Mrkonjic Grad municipality, Milan Malidza presented the conclusions from the meeting held in Banja Luka. First, when you answered this when you were questioned at it before in your own trial, Mr. Malidza attended the 16th Assembly session, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Malidza was a deputy. He was probably at the meeting. He was both a deputy and the municipal president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the strategic goals, if we look at the top of the page, formulated at the meeting in Banja Luka, were presented and it lists them, One, there must be a state separation of the three national communities. Two, the corridor, Krajina must be connected with Serbia, along the bank of the Sava. Three, creation of a corridor along the Drina River valley so that Serbian people control both the left and right bank of the Drina River. And four, establishing the borders of the Una River. Those six strategic goals from two days earlier in Banja Luka, are now being discussed at this meeting, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You can see from this piece of paper that there was some such discussion at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And if we go to the next page, bottom of page 3 in the English, it's on 4 in the B/C/S, at the end of the meeting Colonel Galic proposes implementation of the decisions of the meeting in Banja Luka but submit them to commands of units and municipalities and these conclusions are unanimously adopted. This is now the strategic goals being submitted immediately, two days later, to military commanders in the field, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It is not. This is the only discussion in all of the documents I received that took place after the meeting, and I went through all of the documents when I was in Belgrade. On that day I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This document -- I'm not talking about other documents or documents you couldn't find -- to shows that the goals are disseminated to military leaders, correct? The military is briefed on the strategic objectives, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It is not correct. This was a local meeting at which a deputy informs the audience of the events at the assembly session, and this was not a lonely example. It wasn't the goal per se that people should be informed and disseminated throughout Republika Srpska concerning the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there is no reference anywhere in this document or in some of the other documents we will look at to Mr. Malidza who was present at the session explaining to all these military and local SDS leaders that these are purely political objectives tied to the Cutileiro agreement? In fact, there is a vote to implement these goals on the ground, right? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No. Mr. Prosecutor, on the 9th of June, an order was issued to inform the general public about the strategic goal and the map of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that the same should be disseminated to the international community. In other words an order was issued for that to be disseminated in the general public. I can provide you with the minutes so you can see for yourself. It was on the 9th of June, only a little bit later than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why would that be done on the 9th of June if the entire session, as you say, was open to the public like every session and covered by the press and everybody knew what was announced there already?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This is my conclusion. On the 9th of June, a decision was made to draw an instruction for the implementation of the Geneva Conventions. This was done by Karadzic and Mladic and the Minister of Defence, and it was said, okay, let's inform the general public as to what we want to achieve from the negotiations. Send the strategic goals to the general public, show them the map, and inform the general community, to the European community or international community. I can provide you with the minutes and you can find it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I have time for one more question on this document. The third strategic goal, as published, and basically as discussed -- I'll try to get the exact language -- establishment of a corridor in the Drina River valley and the eradication of the Drina River as a border between the Serbian states. That's what it says in the gazette. You've explained that, if I understood you correctly, that what the third strategic goal was about was ease of border crossing for psychological reasons you shouldn't have to use a passport, you can just use your local ID, right? Did I get your explanation correct of what strategic goal 3 was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's the third strategic goal contains two of our requests to be presented during the negotiations. One was to allow us to have special links and not to have to use passports to cross the Drina. And second of all, an exchange of territories in order to end up with the corridor linking up our corridors and to have a Muslim enclaves across that area. That is the essence of that strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Last question for today: So Milan Malidza, who was present at the 16th Assembly session, got it terribly wrong two days later when he explained what strategic goal 3 was when he said creation of a corridor along the Drina River valley so that the Serbian people control both the left and the right banks of the Drina River; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Every person who interprets a thing interprets that thing the way they find fit at the moment. I'm not saying that this is done on purpose. I'm not saying that he did it on purpose in order to play to the gallery. But he did not interpret the way we envisaged for that strategic goal to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop there for today. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
